nodes.label: Relaxation
nodes.rationale: Every shortest-path algorithm is the same operation applied in a different order — nothing else happens. dist[v] is always the length of SOME path (an upper bound) and relaxation only decreases it; the algorithm terminates when no edge can be relaxed. The choice of which edge to relax next determines both cost and what the algorithm can handle.

nodes.label: Dijkstra's Algorithm
nodes.rationale: Always finalize the closest unfinished vertex; its distance can never improve because reaching it via any other vertex means going further first. The proof step that fails with a negative edge is '<= the whole path's length' — a longer prefix can yield a shorter total, and Dijkstra returns wrong answers with no error. Measured 56.34 ms with a binary heap vs 78.92 s with an O(V^2) scan at V=200k, E=1M (1,401x).

nodes.label: Lazy Deletion in the Priority Queue
nodes.rationale: Push a duplicate on improvement instead of decrease-key, and discard stale entries on pop with `if d > dist[u] { continue; }`. That guard is load-bearing, not an optimization: measured 49% of pops are stale. The usual 'heap grows to Theta(E)' claim is a worst case — measured pushes were 2.0xV, because a vertex is re-pushed only when its distance actually improves, so an indexed heap solves a problem that mostly isn't there.

nodes.label: Bellman-Ford
nodes.rationale: After k rounds dist[v] is correct for every vertex whose shortest path uses at most k edges; a simple path has at most V-1 edges, so V-1 rounds suffice — and a V-th improving round means a reachable negative cycle. That detection is not a bolt-on; it falls out of the invariant.

nodes.label: DAG Relaxation
nodes.rationale: Topological order already guarantees every predecessor is finalized before a vertex is reached — the exact guarantee Dijkstra's heap works to establish. Theta(V+E), allows negative weights, and is the only way to get LONGEST path (by negating). Silently wrong on a cyclic graph, so use Kahn's algorithm which detects the cycle as a by-product.

nodes.label: A* Search
nodes.rationale: Dijkstra with priority dist[v] + h(v). Admissible h (never overestimates) gives optimality; additionally consistent h finalizes each vertex once, exactly as in Dijkstra. With h == 0 it IS Dijkstra.

nodes.label: Floyd-Warshall
nodes.rationale: The k loop must be outermost — it is the DP over 'paths using only intermediates from {0..k}'. Simple, cache-friendly, and genuinely right for V <= ~500; for sparse graphs Dijkstra-from-every-vertex wins, and Johnson's handles negatives by reweighting with Bellman-Ford first.

nodes.label: Integer-Scaled Edge Weights
nodes.rationale: f64 isn't Ord so it can't go in a BinaryHeap without NotNan, and float addition isn't associative — two equal-length paths can compare unequal, making results depend on traversal order. Scaling to millimetres/milliseconds/cents removes both problems.

nodes.label: Infinity Sentinel Overflow
nodes.rationale: u64::MAX is the natural spelling of infinity and also the value that overflows on any addition, so unreached vertices appear at distance ~0 in release. Only fires on disconnected graphs, which random connected test graphs never exercise. Guard the relaxation, use MAX/2, or Option<u64>.

nodes.label: Currency Arbitrage as a Negative Cycle
nodes.rationale: Taking -log(rate) as the weight turns a product condition into a sum condition, so an arbitrage opportunity is exactly a negative cycle — the canonical reason to care about negative-cycle detection.

nodes.label: The Fibonacci Heap Trap
nodes.rationale: Theta(E + V log V) is asymptotically better than a binary heap's Theta((V+E) log V) and loses in practice — pointer-chasing, allocation, and cache behaviour swamp the improvement. Use a binary heap with lazy deletion.
